sections.h2: Can a squatter take ownership of a Wisconsin house?
sections.html:
Yes, but only after meeting every element of a Wisconsin adverse possession statute for a long, uninterrupted stretch. The law sets periods of 20, 10 or 7 years depending on the facts, and the occupant has to prove they fit within one of them.

The title holder starts with the advantage. Under sec. 893.30, a person with legal title is presumed to have been in possession within the time the law requires. Anyone else's occupation is treated as subordinate to that title unless they held the land adversely for 7, 10 or 20 years before a lawsuit. If someone moves into your Wisconsin house without consent, a few months of staying put gains them nothing.

Tenants are a special case. Under sec. 893.31, a tenant's possession counts as the landlord's possession until 10 years after the tenancy ends, or 10 years after the last rent payment when there was no written lease. The adverse possession clocks do not start until that period is over.

The basic period is 20 years. It drops to 10 years when the claimant holds a recorded written instrument, and to 7 years when that claim is paired with payment of every real estate tax.

StatutePeriodMain requirements
Sec. 893.2520 yearsActual continued occupation under claim of title, exclusive of any other right, covering only the part actually occupied that is enclosed by a substantial enclosure or usually cultivated or improved
Sec. 893.2610 yearsEntry in good faith under a written instrument or court judgment, recorded with the register of deeds within 30 days of entry, with continued occupation of a material portion of the land described
Sec. 893.277 yearsThe 10-year requirements, plus recording within 30 days of execution and payment of all real estate taxes for the 7 years after original entry

Claimants can add their time to that of earlier occupants they succeeded, so a claim may rest on more than one person's years. A successful claimant can bring an action under ch. 841 to establish title. Under the 20-year rule a claim reaches only land actually occupied. Under the 10-year rule it reaches the land described in the instrument, except that possession of one lot in a divided tract is not possession of another lot.

Possession means actual, continued occupation under a claim of title. For the written-instrument rules in secs. 893.26 and 893.27, Wisconsin lists facts that show possession, and the list is not exhaustive.

  • The land has been usually cultivated or improved.
  • The land has been protected by a substantial enclosure.
  • Although not enclosed, the land has been used for fuel or fencing timber, or for the ordinary use of the occupant.
  • Where a known farm or single lot is partly improved, the part not cleared or enclosed is treated as occupied for the same time as the improved part, following the usual course and custom of the adjoining country.

Good faith is presumed at entry under the written instrument rules unless someone rebuts it. The 20-year rule has no good faith requirement. A person who enters under a deed they know is fraudulent can still start the 20-year period, but not the 10-year one.

Court decisions attached to the statute add that acts consistent with sporadic trespass do not tell an owner that someone is claiming the land. The test is whether the use gave a reasonably diligent owner notice of an ownership claim.

sections.h2: How can a Wisconsin owner stop an adverse possession claim?
sections.html:
An owner can interrupt the clock by recording an affidavit of interruption, by starting a court action, or by ending the possession in time. Act well before the 20, 10 or 7 years run out.

Sec. 893.305 sets out the affidavit route. The record title holder records an affidavit along with a survey certified no more than 5 years before recording, gives the notice the statute requires, and records proof of that notice. The affidavit gives a legal description, states that the owner is the record title holder, describes the possession being interrupted and says a new period may begin the day after recording. Notice goes by certified mail to a known occupant or neighbor, and by published notice if the person is unknown. When the occupant is a neighbor, the owner must also record a notice of the affidavit against the neighbor's abutting parcel within 90 days after the neighbor receives notice. Recording the affidavit is not an admission that the possession is adverse.

Sec. 893.32 covers entry on the land. A simple entry interrupts a claim only if the owner starts an action against the possessor within one year after the entry and before the limitation period runs, or if the entry actually ends the possession and the owner takes possession. The affidavit procedure is not the only way to interrupt a claim.

Public land is off limits. Under sec. 893.29, no title to land belonging to the state or to a city, village, town, county or school district can be gained by adverse possession.

sections.h2: What to do about a trespasser or someone living in your property
sections.html:
Tell the occupant to leave in clear terms, put the notice in writing, and call local law enforcement if the person stays. Wisconsin defines trespass to land in sec. 943.13, and a violation is a Class B forfeiture.

A person commits trespass by entering enclosed, cultivated or undeveloped land of another without the express or implied consent of the owner or occupant. Entering or remaining after being told by the owner or occupant not to do so is also trespass. The notice can be given personally, orally or in writing, or by posting. Posting means a sign at least 11 inches square in at least 2 conspicuous places for every 40 acres, naming the owner or occupant, or markings that read private land together with the owner's name.

If the occupant was ever a tenant, the circuit court clerk can explain the eviction process. When someone leaves belongings behind in residential rental property, sec. 704.055 requires the landlord to hold them for 7 days from the date they are discovered. After that the landlord may dispose of them, but must return them promptly if the former occupant asks before disposal. The occupant, another owner or a secured party can redeem the property before disposal by paying the landlord's expenses.

Talk to a Wisconsin attorney before you change locks or remove anyone's belongings. If the person refuses to leave, the clerk's office or a lawyer can walk you through the court process.

sections.h2: Selling with a squatter or title dispute
sections.html:
An occupant or a claim to part of the land can slow a sale. Sort out who has the right to be in the house first, and gather your records of ownership, tax payments and any notices you sent.

An owner with an occupant who has no right to be there, a boundary dispute or an unrecorded claim can still sell to a cash home buyer as-is once the title company has reviewed the situation. Ask the buyer's title company what it needs before a closing date is set.

A practical order of work looks like this:

  • Pull your deed and tax payment records and confirm they match the parcel you are selling.
  • Write down when you last visited the property and who has been there since.
  • Send written notice to any occupant and keep a copy.
  • Give the title company the full story so nothing surfaces late in the closing.

If the house is vacant, secure it, keep the taxes current and record any deeds right away. Under sec. 706.08 an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good faith purchaser for value whose conveyance is recorded first.

faqs.q: How many years of occupation does adverse possession need in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: Twenty years under sec. 893.25 in the basic case. It is 10 years if the claimant entered in good faith under a written instrument or judgment recorded within 30 days, and 7 years if the claimant also paid all real estate taxes for the 7 years after entry.

faqs.q: Do squatters have rights to a Wisconsin house after a few months?
faqs.a: No. The shortest adverse possession period in Wisconsin is 7 years, and it requires a recorded instrument and payment of all taxes. A person who stays without consent can be a trespasser under sec. 943.13.

faqs.q: Can someone claim land owned by a city or county in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: No. Sec. 893.29 bars adverse possession of land belonging to the state or to a city, village, town, county or school district.

faqs.q: What should I do with belongings a trespasser leaves behind?
faqs.a: A landlord of residential rental property must hold them for 7 days from the date they are discovered under sec. 704.055. After that the landlord may dispose of them, but must return them promptly if the owner asks before disposal.

faqs.q: Can a tenant claim my Wisconsin property by adverse possession?
faqs.a: A tenant's possession is treated as the landlord's. Under sec. 893.31, the adverse possession periods do not start until 10 years after the tenancy ends, or 10 years after the last rent payment if there was no written lease.
